strengths: Elegant Theoretical Framework: The introduction of Feynman-like diagrams for joint preactivation-NTK statistics is a powerful and elegant way to manage the notoriously tedious algebraic derivations of finite-width corrections (such as those in Roberts & Yaida, 2022). It brings a systematic, visual, and intuitive tool to deep learning theory.

New Analytical Insights: The paper successfully derives several new results, including the first-order correction to the mean NTK, a proof that gradient stability generalizes to finite width (Theorem 5.1), and a proof of the absence of diagonal NTK corrections for scale-invariant activations (Theorem 5.2).

Rigorous Numerical Validation: The authors go beyond pure theory by implementing a custom SymPy-based solver for the complex multi-dimensional Gaussian integrations. The numerical solutions of the recursion relations show remarkable agreement with empirical Monte Carlo simulations, even for relatively small widths (n >= 20).
Generality to All Orders: The authors rigorously prove that the proposed diagrammatic rules are valid not only at order 1/n but generalize to all orders of the finite-width expansion.
weaknesses: Limitation to MLPs: The framework is currently restricted to Multi-Layer Perceptrons. Extending these Feynman rules to more complex architectures (such as CNNs, ResNets, or Transformers), while conceptually possible, is non-trivial and remains future work.

High Computational Cost of Recursion Solvers: Although the diagrammatic method dramatically simplifies the analytical derivation of the equations, evaluating them numerically remains computationally intensive due to high-dimensional Gaussian integration, which may limit practical scalability.

High Entry Barrier: Despite the authors' efforts to make the writing accessible, the QFT-inspired terminology (propagators, vertices, Wick contractions, etc.) may still represent a steep learning curve for a general machine learning audience.

strengths: Elegant and powerful framework: The paper extends the Feynman diagrammatic approach from preactivations to NTK and its higher-derivative tensors, which dramatically simplifies the tedious algebraic derivations associated with finite-width neural networks.

Significant theoretical contributions: The authors derive the recursion relation for the first-order finite-width correction of the NTK mean, prove gradient stability at finite width to all orders of $1/n$, and prove that the diagonal of the NTK mean receives no finite-width corrections to all orders for scale-invariant activations.

Rigorous empirical verification: The authors went through the hard work of numerically implementing the coupled recursion relations (using custom SymPy symbolic code generation and multidimensional integration) and verified them against large-scale Monte Carlo simulations, showing superb agreement.
Excellent presentation: The writing is very clear, the math is rigorous, and the appendices provide detailed proofs and comprehensive experimental setups.
weaknesses: Restriction to MLPs: The framework is currently limited to multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Extending these Feynman rules to CNNs, ResNets, and attention-based models is conceptually possible but remains as future work.

Computational cost of numerical solutions: Solving the coupled recursion relations numerically involves high-dimensional Gaussian integrations, which limits the practical applicability of the solver to networks with few layers and inputs.

Lack of training dynamics: While the finite-width corrections to the NTK are essential for describing feature learning, the paper focuses primarily on initialization statistics and stability, leaving the actual simulation of training dynamics under these corrections for future study.

strengths: First Numerical Solver for 1/n NTK Recursions: The paper successfully implements and solves the highly complex, coupled multi-dimensional numerical integrals for GeLU MLPs at order 1/n, demonstrating excellent agreement with empirical Monte Carlo simulations for widths $n \ge 20$. This represents a significant technical effort.

Novel Theoretical Applications: The authors derive several new results using their framework, including the first-order correction to the NTK mean, a general proof of gradient stability to all orders (Theorem 5.1), and a proof that the diagonal of the NTK mean receives no finite-width corrections for scale-invariant activations (Theorem 5.2).

Rigorous and Extensive Verification: The manuscript is exceptionally thorough, providing a 53-page appendix with detailed step-by-step proofs of the diagrammatic rules and exhaustive experimental details.
weaknesses: Incremental Conceptual Novelty over Prior EFT Frameworks: Much of the mathematical foundation (defining the tensors $A, B, D, F$ and $P, Q, R, S, T, U$ and their role in $1/n$ expansions) was already established in Roberts & Yaida (2022). The introduction of Feynman diagrams for these quantities acts primarily as a post-hoc pictorial translation of these known algebraic equations rather than a fundamentally new theoretical tool.

Extreme Cognitive and Visual Complexity of the Rules: While Feynman diagrams in physics simplify calculations by exploiting physical symmetries, the rules introduced here (especially in Appendix D & E) are incredibly complex. They involve a massive set of ad-hoc conventions (different colored dotted lines, double/triple lines, solid lines, selection rules, pairing rules, etc.). It is highly debatable whether this representation 'dramatically simplifies' the derivations or simply replaces algebraic complexity with equivalent (or greater) graphical complexity.

Highly Limited Practical Utility: Due to the extreme computational cost of solving the coupled multi-dimensional Gaussian integrals numerically, the practical utility of this approach for network architecture design or training dynamics prediction is very limited. The solver is restricted to very shallow MLPs (e.g., depth 4) and small input dimensions, making it hard to apply to modern deep learning contexts.

Architectural Restriction: The framework is strictly limited to MLPs. Extending these Feynman rules to more complex architectures (like CNNs, ResNets, or Transformers) would likely result in an explosion of rules and diagrammatic conventions, rendering the visual approach highly unwieldy.
